A Transformer language model, built from scratch

Tiny Shakespeare GPT

Give it the start of a scene and it writes the rest, one token at a time: a token is a common piece of text, such as “ the” or “ing”. Watch which tokens it is weighing up, and which earlier tokens it is paying attention to, or pick the next token yourself. The model runs on your device, so nothing you type leaves this page.

Where it is looking

The 64 tokens it can see, about 120 characters. Brighter means it paid more attention to that token for this guess, averaged over all 16 attention heads.

lessmore

Is it like ChatGPT?

No. It uses the same core idea, a Transformer that predicts what comes next, but it is about 188,000 times smaller than GPT-3 and only ever read Shakespeare. It was never taught to chat, so it treats a question as the start of a script. Try "Ask a question" to see.

  • Can: keep the format of a play, invent speakers, spell most words, keep the rhythm of verse.
  • Cannot: answer questions, follow instructions, write about a topic you choose, make sense across lines, or remember more than 64 tokens (about 120 characters).
  • Reads bytes: it can take in any text, emoji included, but it only ever saw the characters in the plays, so it rarely writes anything else.

How it writes

Each step, the model looks at the last 64 tokens and scores all 512 tokens it knows: the 256 possible bytes, plus 256 pieces such as “ the” that byte-pair encoding learned by merging the most common pairs in the plays. Softmax turns the scores into the probabilities in the bars, and it picks one at random in proportion to them.

Inside, four Transformer blocks let every token attend to the tokens before it. The attention strip shows where it looked for the current guess. It has no idea what any word means, so it writes things that sound right but rarely make sense.
